title: This 70-Year-Old Hyderabad Shop Bottles Biryani Into a Pickle
excerpt: Qadeem Achar Ghar in Murgi Chowk spent two months perfecting a 20-ingredient, fully vegetarian biryani-flavoured achaar — built for expats missing home.
body:
• Qadeem Achar Ghar, a family-run shop in Hyderabad's Murgi Chowk, sells 16 varieties of achaar — including a pickle flavoured like Hyderabadi biryani.
  • The shop opened in 1954 as a grocery store; pickles began as add-ons and became its most popular product.
  • The biryani pickle took two months of experimentation and uses more than 20 ingredients — cloves, birista fried onion, cardamom, cashews and cinnamon — yet is completely vegetarian.
  • Owner Shaik Huzaifa Al Amoodi says the recipe was created to bring the taste of home back for expats; the shop now ships vacuum-sealed packs with a website and Instagram storefront.

India runs on achaar. Mango, lemon, garlic, mixed vegetable — the pickle jar is the quiet constant on the Indian table, the spoonful that makes everything taste better. But in Hyderabad's Murgi Chowk, a 70-year-old family shop is selling something most Indians have never heard of: a pickle that tastes like biryani.

Qadeem Achar Ghar, which opened in 1954 as a grocery store, now sells 16 different varieties of achaar. Pickles began as mere add-ons to the grocery business, according to Time Out magazine, but they soon became the shop's most popular product. And a few years ago, the family behind the counter set out to do something stranger still: bottle the flavour of Hyderabadi biryani in pickle form.

Two months of trial and error

The biryani pickle was inspired by the city's most famous dish, recreated as a condiment meant to be mixed with rice. Owner Shaik Huzaifa Al Amoodi told Time Out that the family wanted to capture the nostalgia of Hyderabadi biryani in a pickle that could bring the taste of home back for expats.

Getting there took two months of experimentation and several batches to nail the consistency. The final recipe uses more than 20 ingredients, infused with classic spices — cloves, cardamom and cinnamon, birista fried onion, cashews — layered to echo the depth of a proper dum biryani. There is one crucial difference from the dish it imitates: the pickle is completely vegetarian.

"It carries the soul of biryani, reimagined in a way that fits into everyday meals."

— Qadeem Achar Ghar, on Instagram

A family business that moved with the times

The shop is still run by the family — Huzaifa and his two brothers make the pickles themselves. The vegetarian pickles are made fresh twice a week, and the non-vegetarian variants are prepared from scratch every couple of days; during vacations, the store sells up to tens of kilos of non-vegetarian pickles a day.

While the Murgi Chowk address hasn't changed, the business has. The homemade recipes now travel in vacuum-sealed packages, and the shop takes orders through its website and Instagram page. The shelves have expanded too: a variety of papad, mostly lentil- and rice-based, now sits alongside the pickle jars.

Why this works

The biryani pickle lands at the intersection of two Indian obsessions: regional nostalgia and the achaar habit. For Hyderabadis abroad, who have turned "send me achaar" into a standard request for every visitor from home, a pickle that promises the taste of the city's defining dish is an obvious object of affection. It is also shrewd product thinking — achaar is shelf-stable, ships easily, and carries flavour in a way no frozen biryani can match.

Whether it can stand in for the real thing is the wrong question. Achaar was never a substitute; it was always a companion. The biryani pickle simply extends that logic to Hyderabad's most beloved plate, and seventy years in, the family behind Qadeem Achar Ghar still seems to know exactly what its customers want.
